lesson.title: Newcomers and Neighbors: Carpetbaggers, Scalawags, and the Politics of Reconstruction
lesson.summary: White Southern Democrats coined the terms carpetbagger and scalawag as insults for the Northern transplants and Southern Unionists who helped build Reconstruction's biracial governments, labels that shaped how Reconstruction was remembered for generations.
lesson.body:
Reconstruction era Southern Democrats needed a way to discredit the new Republican state governments built on Black votes, and they found one in two vivid insults that stuck for generations: carpetbagger and scalawag. A carpetbagger was supposedly a Northerner who arrived in the South carrying all his belongings in a cheap suitcase made of carpet fabric, implying a man with nothing to lose and everything to gain by looting a defeated region. A scalawag, a much older Southern term for a worthless animal or a rascal, was applied to white Southerners who cooperated with Republican Reconstruction, branding them as traitors to their own region and race.

The reality behind the carpetbagger label was far more varied than the caricature suggested. Many Northerners who moved south after the war were Union veterans who had served there during the fighting and decided to stay, along with teachers and missionaries who came south specifically to build schools for freedpeople, often connected to the Freedmen's Bureau. Others were businessmen and investors drawn by cheap land and the hope of profiting from cotton or the South's postwar railroad building. Some undoubtedly were opportunists looking to exploit a chaotic political and economic landscape, but painting the entire group as parasites ignored the genuine reformers and educators among them.

Scalawags made up an even larger and more complicated group, since they were Southerners choosing to break with their region's dominant political order from the inside. Many had been Unionists during the war, especially in areas like the hill country of Appalachia and northern Alabama where secession had never been popular. Others were small farmers who resented the prewar planter elite's grip on state politics and hoped Republican governments would bring debt relief and broader opportunity, or businessmen who wanted the kind of railroads, banks, and industrial investment they associated with the North. Some scalawags acted out of genuine belief in Black civil rights, though many others supported Reconstruction for practical or economic reasons rather than a commitment to racial equality.

Together with Black voters and the growing number of Black officeholders elected during Radical Reconstruction, carpetbaggers and scalawags formed the political coalition that ran Southern state governments through much of the late 1860s and 1870s. That coalition's dependence on white allies alongside Black voters made scalawags in particular a prime target for the violence of groups like the Ku Klux Klan, who saw them as the weak link that, if intimidated or killed, could break the coalition apart.

The carpetbagger and scalawag stereotypes did not fade with Reconstruction itself. Early twentieth century historians associated with what became known as the Dunning School used these very terms to portray Reconstruction as an era of corrupt misrule imposed on a helpless South, a narrative that helped justify the Redeemer governments that overthrew it. It took the work of later historians, beginning with W. E. B. Du Bois's 1935 study Black Reconstruction in America and continuing through scholars like Eric Foner decades later, to recover a more accurate picture of Reconstruction's real, if incomplete and contested, achievements.
